title: Gotion secures €100 million loan for battery cell factory in Morocco - electrive.com
content:
The African Development Bank has approved a loan of €100 million for the Chinese battery cell manufacturer and Volkswagen partner, Gotion High-Tech. The funds will support the factory Gotion plans to build in Morocco.
Gotion’s new factory is to be built in the Rabat-Salé-Kénitra Free Trade Zone and will be the first integrated battery production facility in Africa. In the first phase, the company is planning an annual capacity of 10GWh for LFP battery cells and packs for use in electric vehicles. In the long term, the aim is to expand capacity to 100GWh.
In 2024, Gotion
signed an investment agreement
with the Moroccan government for the battery cell factory. Gotion Power Morocco, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Gotion, will take the lead on the project. At the time, an initial annual capacity of 20GWh was mentioned. The African Development Bank now states in its press release that the initial capacity will be 10GWh, but confirms a possible later expansion to 100GWh. No details regarding the timetable have been provided.
In addition to the €100 million loan, the bank plans to mobilise further funds from financial partners to support the implementation of this strategic project. The figure being discussed is up to €141 million.
This news is particularly significant for the African continent. A battery plant in neighbouring Morocco could also be a strategic asset for electric vehicle production in southern Europe, particularly within the Spanish cluster.

title: The Chevy Equinox EV is due for an update: Here's what could change
content:
Peter Johnson
| Jul 27 2026 - 8:50 am PT
America’s most affordable 315+ mile range electric vehicle is in line for an update. The next-gen
Chevy Equinox EV
will reportedly be the first to use GM’s all-new platform.
The Chevy Equinox EV is GM’s top-selling electric vehicle in the US. However, with new and heavily updated models like the 2026 Toyota bZ and
Hyundai IONIQ 5
arriving, it’s about time for an upgrade.
After the Equinox EV went on sale in 2024, it quickly caught on with buyers as a long-range (up to 319 miles), practical electric SUV.
Starting at $34,995, it also helped that it was among the most affordable electric vehicles in the US. In its first full sales year, the Chevy Equinox EV was the best-selling electric vehicle in the US outside of Tesla,
ranking third overall
in 2025 behind the Model Y and Model 3.
After the $7,500 federal tax credit expired last September, however, the Equinox lost its cost advantage.
first half of 2026
, Chevy Equinox EV sales are down 41% compared to the period last year, according to the most recent data from Cox Automotive.
While it’s still the fifth most popular EV, the Equinox
slipped behind the Toyota bz
and Hyundai IONIQ 5, both of which received major updates recently.
GM is reportedly already working on its answer. Its current BEV3 architecture underpins the Chevy Equinox EV, Blazer EV, Cadillac Lyriq, Vistiq, and Optiq, as well as the Honda Prologue and Acura ZDX.
Outside of the US, the platform powers GM vehicles in overseas markets, including the Buick Electra E5 and E4 models in China.
The 2023 Cadillac Lyriq was the first to use the third-generation EV architecture. It was designed to incorporate GM’s Ultium batteries and drive motors across a wide range of vehicles, with support for AWD, FWD, and RWD drivetrain configurations.
According to a new report from
GM Authority
, citing sources familiar with the matter, GM is now working on the next evolution of its dedicated EV platform, codenamed BEV-N internally.
While details are still pretty limited, the sources said the first vehicle to arrive on the platform will be the Chevy Equinox EV in late 2028 or early 2029. Following the Equinox, the Chevy Blazer EV will be the next to use the BEV-N platform before it rolls out to other models.
A company spokesperson told
following its
second quarter earnings
last week that GM does “indeed have future EVs in development across all markets,” but didn’t reveal specific models.
GM introduced a dozen EVs, many as 2024 models or newer, so they are still in the middle of their typical product cycles, the spokesperson added. While it has yet to be confirmed, the next-gen Chevy Equinox EV is expected to arrive in either late 2028 or early 2029.
In the meantime, all new 2027 electric vehicles, including the Chevy Equinox, are being updated with an NACS charge port.
The current Chevy Equinox EV already offers an EPA-estimated range of up to 319 miles for FWD models and 307 miles for AWD, but the new platform will likely improve enable it to drive even further on a single charge.
In addition to improved efficiency and faster charging speeds, the new platform is expected to use an advanced software stack, enabling new safety and convenience features.
GM said the Cadillac Escalade IQ will be its first vehicle to offer eyes-off self-driving on highways, starting in 2028. In March, GM said it
began testing
the new automated self-driving tech under “supervised” conditions.
Soon, the company plans to have a fleet of over 200 self-driving and supervised test vehicles on the road.

title: Rivian R2 uses up to 26% more energy than Model Y in real-world test
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 27 2026 - 7:47 am PT
Out of Spec Reviews put a Rivian R2 Performance and a Tesla Model Y Performance on the same roads on the same afternoon. The R2 used 18% to 26% more energy at every single speed they tested.
That’s awkward, because the two SUVs carry identical EPA efficiency ratings, and Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe has been telling media the R2 matches the Model Y.
We covered the ratings when they landed in May: the
R2 Performance matches the Model Y on EPA efficiency
at 105 MPGe combined and 32 kWh per 100 miles. The R2 wins the city cycle 114 to 111. The Model Y wins the highway cycle 100 to 96. And the R2 goes further on a charge, 330 miles against 306.
For a vehicle that weighs roughly 800 lbs more and has the aerodynamic profile of a shoebox, that’s a real engineering achievement.
Scaringe leaned into it at the R2 launch. Asked about the front drive unit disconnect, he told assembled media the R2 is “as efficient on a Wh per mile or miles per Wh basis despite the capabilities it has and despite the form factor that we’ve intentionally chosen to provide the level of utility that it has.”
But EPA ratings are lab numbers. And they rarely match real-world experience.
This part doesn’t get explained often enough, so here it is.
EPA gives EV manufacturers more than one path to a range and efficiency label. The cheap path: run the car on the city cycle until the battery is depleted, run it on the highway cycle until the battery is depleted, then multiply range and fuel economy by 0.7 to approximate real-world driving. EPA’s own guidance says most EVs use that method.
The expensive path is the multi-cycle test: four city cycles, two highway cycles, and two constant-speed cycles, which actually measures cold-weather, hot-weather and high-speed behavior instead of estimating it with a blanket factor. Automakers can also petition EPA for a derived five-cycle method or for adjustment factors based on in-use data. Both require EPA approval.
So a car that runs the longer, costlier test can earn a better correction factor than the flat 0.7. Out of Spec’s Kyle Conner believes that’s what happened here, with Rivian running the R2 through the full procedure at a lab in Michigan while Tesla submitted derived numbers. He says on camera that he can’t certify it, and neither can we. Per-vehicle test paths aren’t published anywhere the public can easily check them, which is its own problem.
There’s a second wrinkle nobody talks about. EPA’s kWh/100 miles figure is measured at the wall, so it includes charging losses. Out of Spec measured energy leaving the battery. Back the label math out and EPA is effectively saying the R2 does about 3.75 miles per kWh from the pack while the Model Y Performance does about 3.64 — EPA has the R2 slightly ahead, and testing put it 18% to 26% behind.
That gap is the whole story.
Methodology first, because it’s the only thing that makes a comparison like this worth reading.
Both SUVs sat until the packs cooled to ambient. Tires set to 42 PSI cold with the same gauge. Climate on auto at 68°F with rear vents off, two occupants per vehicle, screens dimmed, no phone charging. R2 in Conserve, Model Y in Chill. Out-and-back loops at 50, 60, 70 and 80 mph GPS, with the cars swapping the lead each leg so neither one drafted. The two odometers disagreed by about 1.7%, so the comparison ran on kWh consumed rather than the cars’ own efficiency readouts.
Here’s how much more energy the R2 used at each speed, with its own efficiency in brackets:
The 70 mph result breaks the trend, and Conner explains why on camera: that loop ran on I-95 at 5 p.m. in heavy traffic, with both cars picking up slipstream from trucks. Treat it as the soft data point.
Then they built a low-speed city simulation, which is where Rivian’s argument should be strongest. The R2 decouples its front motor with a clutch, so crawling around town it spins one drive unit. The Model Y’s front induction motor keeps turning and paying windage and gear-train losses. Over a 20-minute stop-and-go loop the Model Y used 1.6 kWh and the R2 used 1.9, about 19% worse in the exact scenario built to favor it.
The second video ran Out of Spec’s 10% Challenge: charge from 10% state of charge for exactly 15 minutes, then drive at a constant 80 mph until you’re back to 10%.
The R2 charges well. Really well. Plugged into an
IONNA Rechargery
in Wilson, North Carolina, it held a flat 600 amps, everything the Alpitronic hardware could deliver, all the way to 32% state of charge, peaking around 229 kW. It added 48.3 kWh in 15 minutes for a 193 kW average, going from 10% to 59%. The car asks for up to 630 amps, meaning it was charger-limited rather than battery-limited for that entire window. For a 400-volt architecture, that’s about as good as it currently gets.
Then it drove 92.8 miles at 2.2 mi/kWh. The Model Y Performance, run two days earlier, managed roughly 103 miles at 3.3 mi/kWh on considerably less added energy, because it charges badly and cruises brilliantly.
We wrote the May story off the EPA filings, and those filings said what they said. We’re not walking that back. What this testing exposes is a rating system that let two widely different vehicles land on the same combined number, and then a highway that reminded everyone shapes still matter.
One test day isn’t the last word, and we’d say that even if the result had gone the other way. Out of Spec used in-car energy meters instead of measuring at the charger, ran everything in summer heat on a single day, and had one of four loops compromised by traffic.
But directionally, this is what R2 owners are going to live with, because nobody actually drives the EPA city cycle. People drive 75 on the interstate. At 80 mph the R2 is a 2.2-to-2.5 mi/kWh vehicle and the Model Y is a 3.1-to-3.3 mi/kWh vehicle, and that’s not a rounding error. It makes sense based on the aerodynamic profiles of each vehicle.
The more useful framing is that Rivian made a trade, and it’s a defensible one. The R2 charges better than almost any 400-volt EV you can buy. And while the form factor is much less efficient than the Model Y, it’s also much more SUV, with an emphasis on utility, than Model Y.
came away impressed by the R2 in our first drive
, and this doesn’t change that, but it’s an important data point to consider if you are on the market for a R2. The efficiency figures from the EPA are likely inflated.
This would be a change for Rivian because in general, I found myself more likely to hit EPA efficiency in the R1s than in almost any Tesla vehicle I’ve driven.

title: BMW iX5 LWB debuts with a range of over 620 miles and a huge Theater Screen [Images]
content:
Peter Johnson
| Jul 27 2026 - 7:12 am PT
introduced the new iX5 Long Wheelbase in China with a CLTC driving range of over 620 miles (1,000 km) and plenty of digital screens.
Following the iX3, the iX5 is next in line to receive a Long Wheelbase (LWB) variant. BMW introduced the new X5 and iX5 LWB as standalone models built exclusively for China.
The biggest difference from
the standard X5
, obviously, is the extended wheelbase at 3,165 mm, or 130 mm longer than the version BMW sells in the US, Europe, and other global markets.
Up front, the LWB variant features exclusive “striking diagonal light icons,” while buyers can still opt for BMW’s new double-X design for the iX5 sold elsewhere. Additional light strips are also added between the lights and the illuminated Kidney Iconic Glow grille.
The interior is also redesigned for the Chinese market with a new monochromatic color concept and special seating for front and rear passengers.
Like the iX5 sold elsewhere, the
features BMW’s new Panoramic iDrive display with Panoramic Vision. A passenger screen is also available for the first time in the new X5 and iX5 LWB.
One of the coolest features is the massive BMW Theater Screen for rear passengers, a massive 8K entertainment screen for streaming, gaming, mobile work, and more.
The driver assistance system, developed in partnership with China’s Momenta, is also exclusively built for China with “Address-to-Address” driver assistance. Both models will be equipped with adaptive two-axle air suspension as standard to deliver a premium, smooth ride.
While BMW has yet to reveal full details, it did say the iX5 LWB will deliver a CLTC driving range of over 1,000 km (620 miles). It will officially launch in China in 2027.
Last month, BMW drove an
iX3 50L xDrive (LWB)
over 500 miles (800 km) around the Qinghai Lake grand loop. The prototype achieved an energy consumption of 20.3 kWh/100 miles (12.6 kWh/100 km), or an impressive 4.9 miles per kWh.
In Europe, the iX5 60 xDrive uses a massive 141 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 525 miles (750 km)
EPA estimates have yet to be finalized, but the
2027 BMW iX5 60 xDrive
is expected to offer a range of around 435 miles from a slightly larger 144 kWh battery.

title: Tesla partly settles racism lawsuit as hundreds of workers press on
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 27 2026 - 6:34 am PT
Tesla has confidentially settled with three of the five named plaintiffs in the racism lawsuit that has been hanging over its Fremont factory since 2017.
That doesn’t end much. Up to 580 Black workers are still suing over conditions at the same plant, and California’s civil rights agency is taking its own case to a jury.
The three workers are Marcus Vaughn, who filed the original complaint in 2017 and gave the case its name, plus Titus McCaleb and Monica Chatman. Terms weren’t disclosed. A court filing on June 3 revealed the agreement, and an Alameda County Superior Court judge has ordered the parties back on September 11 to finalize it.
Two named plaintiffs, Garret Parker and Chanel Hendrix, are still in.
So Tesla bought out three people. The case number, RG17882082, is still open, and it’s now the smallest piece of what the company is facing over Fremont.
Here’s how it got this big. In May 2024, the court certified
as a class action covering roughly 6,000 Black workers. Tesla fought the certification and won it back after plaintiffs’ lawyers couldn’t line up enough workers to testify for a manageable trial plan. The judge decertified.
But that didn’t make the claims go away. It just converted one case into many. A state appellate panel later cleared five grouped lawsuits to proceed, and plaintiffs’ counsel says hundreds more workers are holding right-to-sue letters from the state and haven’t filed yet. We
broke down Tesla’s total litigation exposure in April
, and the Fremont race cases were the single largest bloc in it.
This is the part that keeps getting flattened into “racial discrimination lawsuit” in headlines. Strip the dateline off the filings and read them cold, and you’d place them in the Jim Crow South. A segregated worksite, slurs used openly by supervisors, nooses left where Black workers would find them, and firings for anyone who complained. That’s not the 1950s. That’s the factory that built the Model 3.
The workers landed on the same comparison. They called the plant “the plantation” and “the slaveship,” and said the production leads “cracked the whip.”
California’s Civil Rights Department, which sued Tesla in February 2022 after a three-year investigation,
documented specific language in its complaint
: the n-word, “porch monkey,” “monkey toes,” “boy,” “hood rats,” “go back to Africa,” plus the Spanish-language slurs “mayate” and “negrita.” One worker told investigators he heard slurs 50 to 100 times a day.
The agency also alleged the factory was effectively segregated, with an area where Black workers were concentrated known internally as the “porch monkey station.” Workers reported coworkers displaying Confederate flag tattoos to intimidate them.
The EEOC’s own federal complaint, filed in September 2023 in the Northern District of California, adds graffiti: swastikas, threats, and nooses scrawled around the facility, going back to at least 2015. Then-EEOC Chair Charlotte Burrows called it “shameful racial bigotry.”
Among more than 200 worker declarations gathered in the state case, about two-thirds said they saw anti-Black graffiti. Dozens said complaining got them retaliated against, including fired.
One declaration from worker Virshon Meadows describes an older Black woman collapsing on the line. When he went to help, he says a non-Black supervisor told him, “Boy, you better get back on the line.”
Tesla disputes all of it. The company argued in court filings that the workers failed to establish harassment based on race, and submitted declarations from 228 employees who said they saw nothing. Elon Musk has posted about it twice. In 2018 he wrote that “if someone is a jerk to you, but sincerely apologizes, it is important to be thick-skinned.” In 2022 he wrote that “Tesla strongly opposes all forms of discrimination and harassment.”
The state’s case is the one with real teeth, and it survived Tesla’s last exit ramp. On May 27, the court denied Tesla’s motion for summary judgment and cleared the Civil Rights Department’s claims for a jury. Trial was calendared for July 20 in Oakland.
The state isn’t just alleging slurs. It’s alleging Tesla structurally couldn’t handle complaints. CRD found Tesla had 33 HR staff covering 19,916 California workers in 2016, one HR person for every 604 employees, and that the ratio got worse by 2020, hitting roughly one per 740. The department also says Black workers averaged $1,533 less in monthly compensation than white workers between June 2018 and June 2024.
The federal case is quieter, and that’s by design. Tesla and the EEOC agreed in January to move into private mediation, which under the Administrative Dispute Resolution Act means no transcripts and destroyed notes. We
wrote at the time
that it was a smart play for a company that keeps losing in public.
Because it does keep losing in public. A jury hit Tesla with
$137 million in the Owen Diaz case in 2021
. Tesla got it
knocked down to $15 million
, then a retrial produced $3.2 million, then Tesla settled confidentially rather than run it a third time.
Musk has said Tesla would “never settle” a case it finds unjust. He’s said it more than once, publicly, as a matter of principle. Which means every confidential settlement Tesla signs is Tesla saying the quiet part.
That’s the whole problem with the strategy here. Tesla is doing the thing companies do when they think the underlying facts are bad: pay the loudest plaintiffs, seal the terms, push the rest toward mediation, and grind on procedure until the class falls apart. It worked on the class certification. It worked on Diaz, eventually, after two juries. And it just worked on Vaughn, McCaleb, and Chatman.
But it doesn’t scale. You can settle three people. You can’t quietly settle 580, and you definitely can’t settle a state agency that has spent seven years building a record and now has a courtroom date. The CRD case is going to put HR staffing ratios, pay data, and 200-plus worker declarations in front of a jury in Oakland, and Tesla doesn’t get to seal that.
Here’s what we keep coming back to. These allegations run from 2012 to the present. Not one bad supervisor in one bad year. A decade, across the factory that built the cars that made Tesla a household name. Tesla’s answer has been 228 declarations from people who say they didn’t see it and a blog post about being thick-skinned. That’s not a defense. That’s a company hoping the lawyers outlast the workers.
Nine years in, some of them are still there.

title: E-bike bans in schools highlight the growing debate over freedom vs. safety
content:
| Jul 27 2026 - 6:32 am PT
Across the US, school districts are increasingly finding themselves caught in the middle of an uncomfortable question: Should they embrace e-bikes and e-scooters as tools that give students greater transportation independence, or restrict them because of growing safety concerns?
As these vehicles become a more common sight on school commutes, administrators are being forced to balance the freedom they provide families against rising crash statistics, reckless riding, and the reality that many American streets still aren’t particularly safe places for young riders.
A recent example comes to us from a school district in Florida that is voting tomorrow on a policy that perfectly encapsulates one of the biggest debates currently facing micromobility in the US: Are e-bikes and e-scooters empowering young people with new transportation independence, or are they becoming too dangerous to ignore?
According to reporting from the
Orlando Sentinel
, the Orange County School Board is widely expected to approve a policy banning e-bikes and e-scooters from elementary and middle school campuses beginning with the 2026-27 school year. High school students would still be allowed to ride them to school, but only if they have a driver’s license.
The move comes after a difficult year for the district. School officials point to rising injury rates, dangerous riding behavior around campuses, and the tragic death of a 13-year-old student who was struck by a pickup truck while riding an e-scooter to buy Mother’s Day flowers for his mother.
It’s impossible not to sympathize with parents like Ashley LaChance, who now supports the ban after losing her son. No family should have to experience that kind of tragedy.
But the proposal also highlights another reality of the micromobility revolution.
For many families, these aren’t recreational toys for kids to play with after school. Instead, they’re a key form of transportation used to get to school, sports practice, or anywhere else in town that previously relied on being driven around by parents.
One Orlando father interviewed by the
explained that four of his children use e-scooters to travel to three different schools. Living within two miles of campus means they don’t qualify for bus service, while both parents work full-time. The scooters were were purchased specifically to give the children an independent way to get to school.
That story has become increasingly common across the country.
E-bikes and e-scooters have quietly become a form of transportation freedom for teenagers who are too young to drive and for parents trying to juggle work schedules without becoming full-time chauffeurs. They fill a transportation gap that often exists between walking distance and driving age.
Unfortunately, they’re also arriving at the same time that many American roads remain fundamentally designed around cars.
The result is that when children on micromobility devices are injured – or killed – those very e-bikes or e-scooters themselves often become the focus rather than the infrastructure and driver behavior involved in the crash.
To be fair, there are legitimate concerns beyond interactions with cars. Some young riders ignore traffic laws, ride without helmets, carry multiple passengers, or modify already-fast e-bikes into machines capable of much higher speeds. Doctors in the Orlando area report that emergency room visits involving e-bike and e-scooter injuries have risen sharply in recent years, particularly among children aged 10 to 14.
Those statistics shouldn’t be dismissed. But neither should the alternative.
If the response to unsafe roads is simply removing children from e-bikes and e-scooters, the likely replacement isn’t a surge in walking or traditional cycling. More often, it’s another car trip.
Some districts are exploring a different approach. Neighboring Osceola County, for example, has partnered with its sheriff’s office to offer e-bike safety classes instead of prohibiting the vehicles outright. Local governments are also considering helmet requirements, lower speeds around pedestrians, and stronger enforcement of existing traffic laws. The expansion of those
online e-bike safety courses
are often touted as an example of encouraging more e-bike and e-scooter adoption while also ensuring young riders are educated on the rules of the road and safe riding practices.
As e-bikes continue becoming a normal part of American transportation, communities will increasingly have to decide whether the answer is banning them or figuring out how to make riding them safer. For riders and other city residents, the most effective solution may be to preserve the independence these vehicles provide while improving education, infrastructure, and enforcement. That feels like a better long-term solution than simply taking the vehicles away.

title: Musk says Tesla Semi self-driving is a year away, so truckers are safe
content:
Fred Lambert
| Jul 27 2026 - 3:41 am PT
Elon Musk says Tesla expects to have self-driving working on the Tesla Semi “probably around the end of this year or early next year.”
Going by Tesla’s record on self-driving deadlines, it is: their jobs are safe for a long time.
The comment came on Tesla’s Q2 2026 earnings call on July 22, after LightShed analyst Walter Piecyk asked when Tesla would get around to autonomy for the Semi.
Musk opened with the labor shortage. “There just aren’t enough people around who want to drive trucks, which are crucial for transport throughout America,” he said.
Then he framed driverless trucks as a gift to the people who drive them: “making it easier on truck drivers to have a self-driving Semi is going to dramatically improve safety and comfort for truck drivers that use the Tesla Semi.”
These two statements sort of clash together because FSD won’t help with the shortage of truckers if you still need them inside the truck, just like FSD in consumer vehicles. Ultimately, Musk is talking about full autonomy inside Tesla’s semi trucks.
And the timeline: “We expect to get self-driving working on the Tesla Semi probably around the end of this year or early next year.”
In the same answer, he said Tesla is focusing its self-driving work on its high-volume vehicles — Model 3, Model Y, and Cybercab — and that Semi autonomy is “taking a bit of a backseat for the next six months or so.”
So it’s a year out, and nobody is really working on it for the next six months. Sure.
Here’s the problem with a one-year Musk timeline on autonomy.
We charted his prediction record earlier this year using data from MuskOmeter, which tracks 94 public Musk predictions. Eight of them were delivered on time. That’s 9%. Another 46 failed outright.
Self-driving is his worst category. We count roughly 10 self-driving and robotaxi deadlines since 2013, and every single one that has come due has been missed.
In October 2016, he said a Tesla would drive itself from Los Angeles to New York by the end of the following year. That was nine years ago and it still hasn’t happened. He said FSD would be “feature complete” by the end of 2019. He promised 1 million robotaxis on the road by 2020. In July 2020, he was “100% confident” Tesla would solve Level 5 autonomy the next year.
Last year it was robotaxi service for half the US population by December. This January it was Europe and China approving FSD “next month.”
The live promise right now is unsupervised FSD on customer cars in Q4 2026, which Musk
repeated again in May
and which we’ve
gone through in detail
If a year of Musk time on self-driving has historically meant closer to a decade, truck drivers are covered into the 2030s.
The Semi was supposed to have this already.
Tesla unveiled it in November 2017 with “Enhanced Autopilot” and a demo of convoy mode, where trucks follow each other autonomously down the highway. Production was promised for 2019.
It slipped to 2020, then 2021, then 2022. A handful of trucks went to PepsiCo at the end of that year, and at the delivery event,
Tesla didn’t mention Autopilot or self-driving once
. Convoy mode quietly came off the website.
The first Semi built on Tesla’s high-volume line at Giga Nevada rolled out
. That factory is designed for 50,000 trucks a year. Tesla told investors this week that the Semi will still be “a very small percentage” of its total vehicle fleet by the end of 2026.
The trucker-shortage framing is the part worth sitting with. In 2022, Tesla scrubbed every mention of autonomy from its Semi marketing, and the read at the time was that Tesla needed drivers and fleet managers to want this truck. Now the driverless version is back as a feature, and it’s being sold as safety and comfort for the driver whose seat it eliminates.
The companies actually running driverless trucks don’t bother with that pitch. Aurora has been hauling freight on Texas highways with nobody in the cab, crossing 250,000 driverless miles in March and targeting more than 200 trucks this year.
As for Tesla, the company has racked up only 380,000 unsupervised miles in a year of testing unsupervised self-driving in its robotaxi service in Texas. And to limit the damage, the company has focused on a lower-speed, geo-fenced area.
I think it will be a while before it feels confident enough to increase the speed and the geo-fenced area to a degree that it makes sense for the Tesla Semi.

title: Croatia’s first energy community begins sharing solar power - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
A community in northern Croatia has become the first in the country to benefit from new regulations governing energy communities. The 17 members share solar energy from a rooftop array located on a voluntary fire department.
Patrick Jowett
Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Image: REGEA
Croatia’s first energy community is now operational. The community utilizes a rooftop solar plant on the building of the volunteer fire brigade in Špičkovina, a settlement near Zabok in the county of Krapina-Zagorje, northern Croatia.
The project, implemented by the North-West Croatia Regional Energy and Climate Agency (REGEA), features a rooftop solar array currently 32 kW in size, with plans to double the capacity to 64 kW.
The community has 17 members in total, consisting of volunteer firefighters, local residents, one micro-enterprise and the voluntary fire department itself, named DVD Špičkovina.
Ivana Belić, Head of Strategic Communications at REGEA, explained to
the community operates on an energy-sharing model, without on-site storage, that differs from conventional self-consumption.
“The electricity is not consumed behind a single meter. Instead, the output of the plant is distributed through the public grid to the metering points of the community members, according to a fixed allocation key,” Belić explained. “Each member’s share is credited against the consumption recorded at that member’s own metering point. Members expect their electricity bills to fall substantially, by roughly half.”
The City of Zabok co-financed around half of the investment, while the members financed the other half, which Belić says halved each member’s own outlay. She added that the purpose of the energy community is to benefit the community rather than generate commercial profit.
“Membership is open and voluntary, and the members keep control of the organisation,” Belić said. “A volunteer fire brigade is a natural host for this model. In Croatia, volunteer fire brigades are long-standing local institutions with a public role and a building that serves the whole settlement. The value created by the solar plant stays in the local community.”
Energy sharing is the newest part of Croatia’s energy legislation, with Croatia’s distribution system operator, HEP ODS, introducing the mechanism at the start of April this year.
The Renewable Energy Sources of Croatia (RES Croatia) told
the move marked the most important prerequisite for energy communities to become operational. “However, there are still several administrative barriers that need to be simplified, and we expect further regulatory improvements in the near future,” the association said.
There are currently three energy communities officially registered in Croatia, RES Croatia added, with the Špičkovina community the first to begin operations.
“We certainly expect this segment to grow. According to the latest public opinion survey, 71% of Croatian citizens would like to produce electricity together with their neighbours, for example through a shared rooftop solar installation,” the association told
. “In addition, the Croatian Energy Regulatory Agency has recently launched a public consultation on a new regulatory framework aimed at supporting citizen energy initiatives.”
Belić added that the experience gained from the Špičkovina energy community, from the registration of the community to the grid procedures and allocation of shared electricity, is directly useable by other Croatian communities.
“The importance of Špičkovina is not its size,” Belić said. “It proves that energy sharing works under Croatian rules, and it gives other communities a tested path to follow.”

title: French residential solar market suffers sharp 2025 downturn - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
French residential solar installations fell sharply in 2025, according to a report by independent research organization Observ’ER, following regulatory and tariff changes that reshaped the small-scale segment.
François Puthod
Markets & Policy
Image: Pixabay
Sales volumes for installations under 3 kW dropped 45.4% year-on-year to 153,250 kW in 2025, while the 3 kW to 9 kW segment fell 17.6%, from 685,000 kW to 564,100 kW, according to Observ’ER’s annual report on small-scale solar applications. The decline follows eight consecutive years of growth from 2017 to 2024, during which the market grew by more than 43% annually on average — marking the sector’s first severe slowdown since 2011.
Observ’ER attributed the downturn to regulatory changes introduced in 2025. Since March of that year, installations between 0 kWp and 9 kWp have no longer been eligible to sell their full solar output to utility EDF OA under the obligation d’achat scheme, and can now sell only their surplus, unconsumed electricity. The feed-in tariff for that surplus also collapsed, falling from €0.12 to €0.01 per kWh. Self-consumption incentives were also significantly reduced.
Observ’ER said the uncertain economic climate in 2025 further weighed on household investment, which accounts for the majority of small-scale solar installations.
Average system prices also fell in 2025, dropping 7.3% for a 3 kW installation to an estimated €2.15 per watt excluding tax, including installation but not storage equipment. Equipment prices, particularly for modules and inverters, fell 11.7%, while labor costs rose 5%, driven mainly by wage increases to offset recent inflation.

title: Costa Rica starts connecting 20 MW solar project - pv magazine Global

Applications & Installations
Markets & Policy
Utility-scale
The Costa Rican Electricity Institute (ICE) has begun the process of connecting the Los Tecales photovoltaic solar plant to Costa Rica’s national electricity system.
ICE is conducting technical tests to verify the proper functioning of the equipment and its integration with the national grid. Once this process is complete and compliance with the system’s operating standards is verified, the plant can begin commercial operation.
The 20 MW plant, developed by Solar Generation Sur SA, is located in the canton of Nandayure within the province of Guanacaste. It is part of a group of
five private photovoltaic projects awarded by ICE in April 2024
, with a combined installed capacity of 86 MW.
The other projects are Numu (20 MW), Colorado (16 MW), Los Mangos (10 MW), and Las Cañas (20 MW). They are all located in the province of Guanacaste and were awarded with an energy purchase price of $0.05626/kWh.
The awarding of these projects is part of the renewable energy expansion plan announced by ICE in 2024, which includes the addition of 270 MW of solar capacity between 2024 and 2026, along with 122 MW of wind power and 20 MW of biomass.
The strategy aims to meet the projected growth in electricity demand, diversify the generation mix, and strengthen the country’s energy security in the face of increased hydrological variability.
In addition to these private projects, ICE is moving forward with the development of its own photovoltaic power plants, including
the 66 MW Colorado ICE and 78 MW Las Delicias projects
, alongside the 10 MW San Antonio project.
Costa Rica had installed 83 MW of solar by the end of last year, according to figures compiled by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), a 10 MW increase on the year prior.

title: AusNet sidesteps global supply chain concerns with transformers contract - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Australian network operator AusNet has struck a AUD 300 million ($210 million) deal with South Korea’s Hyosung Heavy Industries to secure the supply of up to 45 power transformers to strengthen the energy network in the state of Victoria.
David Carroll
Technology & Products
Image: AusNet
AusNet has signed a long-term supply contract with Hyosung Heavy Industries to secure the supply of up to 45 ultra-high-voltage power transformers as it works to strengthen Victoria’s transmission network, support the continued growth of renewable energy generation in the state and growing electricity demand.
Under the agreement, valued at about AUD 300 million , Hyosung will supply AusNet with 45 transmission transformers – needed to step voltage up or down across the grid – reactors and other critical power equipment over the next five years.
AusNet Chief Executive Officer David Smales said the Hyosung deal is essential to delivering Victoria’s future energy system, adding that the contract reduces supply chain risk and guarantees access to equipment that will
improve network reliability
and provide greater certainty for the delivery of solar, wind and battery projects across Victoria.
“Transformers are a critical enabler of the energy transition,” he said. “This agreement locks in access to
globally scarce equipment
, giving us greater certainty to deliver critical projects.”
“Around the world, energy companies are competing for a limited pool of equipment. By acting early and partnering with a trusted supplier like Hyosung, we can secure the infrastructure we need while managing cost pressures for Victorian households and businesses.”
Victoria has established renewable energy generation and storage targets, including 65% renewable energy generation by 2030 and 95% by 2035. It also aims to achieve at least 6.3 GW of energy storage by 2035, with an interim target of 2.6 GW by 2030. Decentralised generation is also expected to grow, with rooftop solar connected to AusNet’s distribution network forecast to increase by more than 20% by 2031.
Hyosung Chairman Cho Hyun-joon said the state’s energy transition is driving rising demand for advanced grid stabilisation and high-voltage equipment with Australia as a whole firming as a key strategic market for the company.
“Australia is one of the most dynamic markets in the world in terms of both the pace and scale of energy transition,” he said, adding that Hyosung “will continue expanding cooperation into next-generation grid solutions, such as high-voltage direct current systems, positioning ourselves not merely as an equipment supplier, but as a partner helping drive Australia’s energy transition.”

title: Solar for Ukraine campaign continues to save lives - pv magazine Global
content: By the end of this year, the Solar for Ukraine campaign aims to help at least a dozen hospitals in Ukraine obtain photovoltaic systems capable of providing emergency power. “If donations allow, even more,” says the Biohaus Foundation, which has been organizing the campaign together with Greenpeace Germany and Greenpeace Ukraine since mid-2024. It doesn’t take much imagination to grasp what’s at stake: power outages in a hospital that last hours rather than minutes, and strike almost daily rather than once every few years. Where emergency generators are overwhelmed or unavailable due to lack of fuel, it’s no exaggeration to say that a photovoltaic system on a hospital can save lives. Yet despite, or perhaps because of, those high stakes, the campaign takes a surprisingly pragmatic approach, one shaped by the need to use available funds as effectively as possible. “We no longer want to send used modules to Ukraine” is one statement that might seem puzzling at first. However, Willi Ernst, who co-founded the Biohaus Foundation with Dagmar Schmidt-Gold in 2009 and was previously among Germany’s solar pioneers with his company Biohaus PV, which he sold in 2006, can explain the logic behind it. While no one wants to give the cold shoulder to people who would like to put such used modules to good use, Ernst explained that one of the biggest and, above all, costliest problems is transportation and old modules with their low efficiency ratings increase the cost per kilowatt. The campaign has benefited from the fact that at the end of last year and the beginning of this year, many photovoltaic companies still had 400 W modules in stock, brand new but hard to sell. Quite a few of these are now in use in Ukraine. Every bit of help is also a market entry Ernst points to other pragmatic considerations shaping the campaign, such as the search for sponsor companies willing to help with training, system planning, or other support. These companies, he notes, are also likely to benefit themselves, since “every bit of help is, in a sense, a market entry.” He’s not alone in believing Ukraine will be an important long-term market: its solar sector was already gaining momentum before the Russian invasion in February 2022, and the war has only reinforced, for many Ukrainians, the value of decentralized power. The emphasis on decentralization explains another pattern: the Solar for Ukraine campaign is often offered inverters, but has to turn down many of them, and in particularly grid-connected models. “Because of the situation in Ukraine, we can hardly build grid-connected systems anymore,” Ernst says, pointing to the Russian military’s repeated attacks on the country’s infrastructure. That’s why the hospitals selected by Solar for Ukraine are equipped with systems capable of providing emergency power, with a typical set up consisting of 60 kW module capacity, a 40 kW hybrid inverter and a 72 kWh battery storage system. A solar company for after the war, too Every installed system has to be tailored as much as possible to the needs of its specific location. It also has to be installed and maintained. These practical demands helped give rise to another initiative connected to the campaign: SolarWomen4Ukraine, which aims to build its own company. Around 30 women have already completed basic training with Greenpeace’s support. Here, too, the reasoning is pragmatic rather than symbolic: women aren’t the focus because the foundation wants to open up the solar installer profession to them specifically, but because so many men are away at war. In any case, according to Ernst, the company should by no means be limited to the hospital projects, but should also “look for customers in the regular market.” Companies willing to help, for example, by supporting the training of a female installer in Germany, are actively being sought after, as is anyone able to donate materials, including tools ranging from I-V curve tracers to screwdrivers. And underlying all of this, as always, is the need for money. Reaching the current goal of twelve hospitals equipped with solar power isn’t the end of the effort — it’s just the start, since, as Ernst puts it, there are “about 100 more now waiting.” The post Solar for Ukraine campaign continues to save lives appeared first on pv magazine Global .

title: Lebanon tenders 350 MW of solar - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
A tender is open in Lebanon covering five grid-connected solar projects with a combined capacity of 350 MW, to be paired with up to 1 GWh of battery storage. The deadline to submit expressions of interest is August 31.
Patrick Jowett
Markets & Policy
Asia-Pacific
Energy Storage
Utility-scale
Image: Ahmad Bader/Unsplash
The Electricity Regulatory Authority (ERA) of Lebanon has kicked off a tender for up to five grid-connected solar projects.
Tender details
state the solar projects will have an installed capacity of 350 MW and will be tied to battery energy storage systems (BESS) totalling 1 GWh. The location and exact capacity of each of the projects is yet to be published.
Chosen developers will be responsible for land acquisition or leasing, all required permits and project design, as well as the financing, construction, interconnection, testing, commissioning and long-term operation and maintenance of the project.
The tender also features a call for distributed dual-fired thermal power plants that operate on natural gas as the primary fuel. The plants are expected to have net capacities ranging from 20 MW to 100 MW.
Projects are expected to be structured under an independent power producer model, the tender adds, with any future contractual arrangements, such as power purchase agreements, at the discretion of the relevant public authority.
The tender opens with an expressions of interest stage, with prospective developers asked to submit their documentation electronically by August 31. ERA says the information received will support the preparation of subsequent licensing, procurement and project implementation phases.
Lebanon’s cumulative solar capacity stood at 1,505 MW by the end of 2025, according to figures published by the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA), up from 1,081 MW at the end of 2024.

Albania is set to allow agrivoltaics under certain conditions following approved amendments to its law governing agricultural land, with its council of ministers tasked with determining the applicable criteria.

The government of Albania has adopted amendments to its law governing agricultural land to allow agrivoltaics to be developed on specific categories of land. The revision also permits wind energy plants and storage systems on agricultural land under certain conditions.
The amended article, available on the Albanian government’s website, says the council of ministers shall determine the criteria and conditions under which agricultural land can be used for agrivoltaics.
Ministers will also be responsible for establishing the procedures for monitoring the installations, including measures for any violations against the rules, as well as the fee to be paid by entities selling electricity produced by agrivoltaics.
“The fee shall be transferred to a program for agriculture and rural development [in order] to support agriculture,” the article states.
The legislation was approved with 77 votes in favour, with the majority of the rest of the 140 members of Albania’s parliament abstaining.

title: New disaggregation methodology quantifies uncertainty in behind-the-meter PV generation - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Researchers in Spain have developed a conditional diffusion-based model to improve the visibility of behind-the-meter PV systems using low-resolution smart meter data. The probabilistic approach enables accurate PV reconstruction with uncertainty estimates, helping distribution system operators better manage grid planning and flexibility.
Emiliano Bellini
Research & Development
Image: pv magazine / AI generated
The rapid adoption of behind-the-meter (BTM) distributed energy resources, such as photovoltaic (PV) systems and heat pumps (HPs), is creating new challenges for distribution system operators (DSOs). Since these assets are located behind customer meters, their individual generation and consumption profiles are not directly observable from conventional smart meter measurements. This lack of visibility limits DSOs’ ability to accurately assess network conditions, forecast demand, and manage emerging flexibility opportunities.
Addressing this challenge, a research team from Spain’s Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya (UPC) has introduced a generative diffusion-based methodology for probabilistic BTM PV disaggregation. The method extracts the probabilistic characteristics of PV generation from low-resolution smart meter data, enabling reconstruction of solar production profiles from measurements available at 30-minute intervals.
“Our work started from a real request,” corresponding author Marc Jené Vinuesa told
. “A Spanish DSO asked us for a service to estimate voltage volatility on their network, but it had no knowledge of which PV systems were installed behind the meter in their grid, which is exactly the input such a service needs. That gap is what the method addresses: the DSO first gains visibility of what is installed, and from there, several data-driven services become possible. We like to say the method serves as a service enabler.”
Dubbed conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (cDDPM), the proposed method learns the distribution of daily PV generation profiles using low-resolution smart meter data, net consumption, and local irradiance information. During inference, the model generates multiple plausible PV profiles, enabling probabilistic estimates with uncertainty intervals. These generated samples enable both point estimates and uncertainty quantification through probabilistic intervals.
The model is conditioned on available information such as net consumption, irradiance, and location-related features to improve reconstruction accuracy. During inference, the diffusion model generates PV profiles by progressively denoising random noise while preserving temporal characteristics of daily generation patterns. A 1D U-Net architecture is employed as the noise prediction network, incorporating time embeddings and conditioning signals to capture complex temporal dependencies.
The new method was trained and evaluated using two real-world residential datasets from Australia and the Netherlands. The Australian dataset includes 257 PV-equipped households with one year of half-hourly smart meter and PV generation data, while the Dutch dataset is used to assess cross-region generalization. The model performance is evaluated using both deterministic metrics, such as RMSE, MASE, MAPE, and SMAPE, and probabilistic metrics, including prediction interval coverage, sharpness, and quantile accuracy.
Several baseline methods are considered, including physics-based, proxy-based, ensemble, quantile regression, and conditional variational autoencoder approaches. The proposed cDDPM model is trained using a 1D U-Net architecture and optimized through extensive hyperparameter tuning. Experiments are conducted on high-performance computing infrastructure to ensure reliable training and evaluation. The methodology is tested across multiple train–test splits to assess robustness and seasonal variability. The evaluation focuses on both the accuracy of PV reconstruction and the reliability of uncertainty estimates. Overall, the experimental framework provides a comprehensive comparison between the diffusion-based approach and existing deterministic and probabilistic disaggregation techniques.
The model performance is evaluated using both deterministic metrics, such as Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), and Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (SMAPE), as well as probabilistic metrics, including Prediction Interval Coverage Probability (PICP), Prediction Interval Normalized Average Width (PINAW) for uncertainty sharpness, and Pinball Loss (PL) for quantile accuracy.
Experiments were conducted on high-performance computing infrastructure to ensure reliable training and evaluation, with the methodology being tested across multiple train–test splits to assess robustness and seasonal variability.
The analysis showed that the cDDPM offers superior performance for behind-the-meter (BTM) PV disaggregation compared with deterministic and probabilistic benchmark methods. Calibration analysis confirmed that the uncertainty estimates remain reliable, particularly during periods of active PV generation. Further analysis showed that combining irradiance with current and previous-day net consumption improves both accuracy and uncertainty estimation.
Vinuesa explained that the model could also be used for PV-driven homes including batteries and electric vehicles (EVs). “Accurate PV disaggregation in PV-plus-battery homes would require training the model with representative datasets that include battery-equipped households,” he went on to say. “Our previous work demonstrated that conditioning the model on irradiance alone can still achieve competitive PV disaggregation performance, which may become particularly relevant in scenarios where battery operation obscures the relationship between PV generation and net consumption.”
He also stated that, compared with batteries, EV charging is expected to have a smaller impact on PV disaggregation because most residential charging occurs during evening and nighttime periods, when PV generation is negligible. “However, the interaction becomes more complex as smart charging strategies increasingly align EV charging with periods of high solar availability,” he added. “In such cases, additional information, such as electricity prices, charging behavior, or user preferences, may be required. Furthermore, if the objective shifts from PV disaggregation alone toward the simultaneous identification of multiple flexible resources—including EV consumption, battery charging/discharging, and heat pump operation—the model would need to incorporate additional exogenous variables and be trained on more diverse multi-resource datasets.”
The new methodology was presented in “
Conditional diffusion modeling for probabilistic behind-the-meter PV disaggregation
,” published in
Energy and AI

title: India's Advait Greenergy, China's GuofuHee showcase 5 MW alkaline electrolyzer - pv magazine Global

Indian clean energy engineering company Advait Greenergy (AGPL) and China’s Jiangsu Guofu Hydrogen Energy Equipment (GuofuHee), AGPL’s electrolyzer technology partner, jointly conducted a live factory acceptance test and technical demonstration of a 5 MW pressurized alkaline water electrolysis system at GuofuHee’s manufacturing facility in Zhangjiagang, China. demonstration gave customers and industry stakeholders the opportunity to evaluate electrolyzer technology under real operating conditions.

title: World's largest offshore converter station installed off China's coast
content:
China has just installed the world’s largest offshore converter station off the coast of Guangdong, which is set to transmit roughly six billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) of clean electricity every year
Known as the ‘Heart of Offshore Wind” the massive platform will collect electricity generated by offshore wind farms and efficiently deliver it to the mainland grid. It was installed on Thursday, July 23, about 62 miles (100 kilometers) from the coast of Yangjiang in the South China Sea.
The facility is reportedly the world’s first 500-kilovolt (kV), 2,000-megawatt (MW) flexible direct current (DC) offshore converter station. The project has now moved into the final phase of subsea cable installation and offshore-onshore joint testing before commercial operation starts.
Once fully commissioned, it is expected to reduce carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions by nearly five million metric tons annually. It took about seven hours to complete the installation.
China’s State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission (SASAC), which is responsible for managing state enterprises, disclosed that the converter station is made up of
two massive structures
. The first one includes a seven-story steel superstructure. The second is a jacket foundation anchored to the seabed.
The upper platform is 280 feet (85.5 meters) long, 271 feet (82.5 meters) wide and 144 feet (44 meters) tall. It weighs about 25,000 metric tons. It is supported by the jacket foundation, which measures 269 feet (82 meters) long, 187 feet (57 meters) wide and 226 feet (69 meters) high. The structure weighs 17,000 metric tons.

At the same time, the structure is also secured to the seabed by a total of eight foundation piles. These are designed to withstand
strong winds
, powerful waves, ocean currents, corrosive saltwater, dense sea fog and frequent typhoons.
The converter station’s enormous weight far exceeded the lifting capacity of any domestic vessel, forcing engineers to develop an
innovative installation method
. This is why engineers adopted an approach known as “float-over” installation.
Instead of lifting the massive steel platform directly into place, the engineers used the semi-submersible heavy-lift vessel,
Xiang Tai Kou
. They then slowly positioned the structure over its jacket foundation.
The process relied on the tidal movements and the vessel’s dynamic positioning system to guide the platform into place with remarkable precision. During the operation, the clearance between the upper structure and the foundation was only six inches (150 millimeters) on each side.
the rubber fenders
and specialized coupling devices installed on the foundation legs helped absorb potential impacts. They also ensured the platform aligned safely before being secured. The installation took seven hours to finalize.
Project teams closely monitored forecasts from multiple weather services before selecting an installation window with favorable wind and sea conditions. The operation began shortly after 7 am on June 4.
“The Heart of the Sea Wind converter station has the world’s highest voltage and largest transmission volume of offshore wind power, flexible DC transmission projects,” SASAC revealed in a
press release
. Once operational, it will deliver six billion kWh of clean electricity annually while cutting CO2 emissions by nearly five million metric tons.

title: China uses fast-growing bamboo barriers to fight desertification
content:
Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Forestry are introducing bamboo-based barriers and trays to stabilize shifting sands. It could offer an eco-friendly alternative to existing sand-fixing methods.
This strategy replaces short-lived straw grids and non-biodegradable plastics with woven bamboo barriers and rainwater-collecting trays.
South China Morning Post (SCMP)
reported that these renewable bamboo systems are expected to extend barrier lifespans from a few years up to a decade and reduce overall costs by over 20 percent.
Desertification
is the severe degradation of fertile drylands into unproductive, desert-like terrain, stripping the soil of its vegetation, nutrients, and agricultural capability.
Driven by practices like overgrazing and
deforestation
alongside climate pressures, this land loss poses a massive ecological and human threat. As evidenced in China, where desertification now affects 27.4% of the nation’s land area and directly impacts around
400 million people
Earlier measures to combat desertification across its arid northern regions included sand-fixing methods like straw, plastic barriers, and pollen-heavy shrubs.
For instance, take China’s
Taklimakan Desert
, which is the world’s second-largest mobile desert.

content:
The Royal Navy is testing a robotic boat capable of autonomously launching and recovering a drone at sea, in a demonstration aimed at expanding uncrewed maritime surveillance.
British maritime robotics company ACUA Ocean and US-based Teledyne FLIR Defense conducted two days of trials for the UK Ministry of Defence and offshore industry partners.
The system combines an uncrewed surface vessel (USV) with a tethered uncrewed aerial system (T-UAS), allowing the boat to deploy an airborne sensor without human intervention.
The demonstration was supported by UK Defence Innovation (UKDI), which funds emerging technologies with potential military applications.
The Royal Navy is exploring a new approach to persistent maritime surveillance by combining an autonomous drone launch system with an uncrewed surface vessel (USV), allowing aerial reconnaissance to continue for extended periods without putting personnel at risk.
At the center of the demonstration were Teledyne FLIR Defense’s SkyCarrier and SkyRanger R70, working alongside ACUA Ocean’s Pioneer USV. SkyCarrier is an autonomous drone launch-and-recovery system housed in a protective container that unfolds into an articulating landing pad. During the trial, it autonomously launched and recovered the SkyRanger R70 from the deck of the Pioneer, even as the vessel operated at sea, reports

The SkyRanger R70 remained connected to the Pioneer through a managed power and data tether. Rather than relying solely on its onboard battery, the drone received continuous power from the vessel, enabling longer-duration aerial surveillance. The tether also keeps the aircraft positioned above the USV, allowing it to maintain a persistent view of the surrounding area without independently flying away.

title: Quantum Heat Waves Spotted at Room Temperature for the First Time
content:
The discovery could improve thermal management in electronics and support advances in quantum and next-generation computing technologies.
Heat usually spreads outward through a solid, making it difficult to control once it begins moving. Until now, a wavelike form of heat transport called phonon focusing had been observed only at extremely low, or cryogenic, temperatures, sharply limiting its study and possible applications.
Researchers at the
Samueli School of Engineering
have now shown that phonons, quantum vibrations that carry heat through a material, can travel along concentrated, ray-like paths at room temperature. Rather than dispersing evenly in every direction, the heat followed routes determined by the underlying crystal structure, suggesting a new way to direct thermal energy in future electronics and quantum technologies.
The work, published in
Nature Physics
, was led by Yongjie Hu, a professor of mechanical and aerospace engineering at UCLA Samueli. His group observed room-temperature phonon focusing in boron arsenide, a crystalline semiconductor known for its high thermal conductivity.
Instead of waiting for unwanted heat to spread and then trying to remove it, boron arsenide could potentially steer that energy along carefully chosen routes with
precision, similar to how optical fibers direct light.
The researchers developed a nanoscale temperature mapping method to make the effect visible. Ordinary materials produced circular temperature patterns, showing the familiar process in which heat diffuses outward.
Boron arsenide behaved differently. Its temperature patterns formed distinct rays, revealing that heat was traveling preferentially along specific directions within the crystal.
The pattern changed in predictable ways when the orientation of the crystal changed. Different planes within boron arsenide produced sixfold, eightfold, and fourfold arrangements of focused heat.
This quantum phonon behavior persisted across distances of one micrometer and could potentially extend for tens of micrometers. That range is large enough to be relevant for many electronic, photonic, and quantum devices.
“This is a fundamental observation that enables us to think about thermal management in a new way,” said Hu, the study’s corresponding author and a member of the California NanoSystems Institute at UCLA. “By enabling heat to be guided, focused and redistributed with nanoscale precision at room temperature, the discovery establishes a foundation for quantum thermal engineering.”
The ability to control heat at atomic scales could help address overheating in AI hardware, microelectronics, aerospace systems and other devices where rising temperatures restrict performance, reliability and scalability.
Hu said the finding may also allow researchers to adjust interactions between phonons, electrons and other carriers of energy. Such control could benefit future quantum information and sensing technologies.
Earlier demonstrations of phonon focusing largely required temperatures only a few degrees above
absolute zero
. Under those conditions, phonons can travel long distances without frequently colliding or scattering.
At room temperature, phonons generally scatter much more often and rapidly lose their wave coherence, causing heat to spread through conventional diffusion.
The new findings build on Hu’s earlier work involving the
experimental discovery
of boron arsenide in 2018. His group has since demonstrated
high-performance thermal interfaces
allium nitride devices that incorporate boron arsenide for cooling
, underscoring the material’s potential for future semiconductor technologies.
Boron arsenide experiences unusually weak phonon scattering, allowing wavelike heat transport to survive even at room temperature.
The measured heat patterns agreed with theoretical predictions, confirming that phonons can travel unusually far before scattering — the essential condition that makes this room temperature wave behavior possible.
Reference: “Phonon focusing at room temperature” by Man Li, Huan Wu, Zihao Qin, Chuanjin Su, Huu Duy Nguyen and Yongjie Hu, 23 July 2026,
Nature Physics
DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03335-y

title: Invisible Black Holes Could Be Triggering Supernovae
content:
Primordial black holes may trigger some
explosions and leave measurable signatures in the
’s chemistry.
Some Type Ia supernovae may begin with an invisible intruder passing through a white dwarf. An international research team has found that primordial black holes could trigger these stellar explosions and leave behind chemical patterns observed in the Milky Way. The study was published in
Astrophysical Journal
Primordial black holes (PBH) are hypothetical remnants of the early universe that may have formed from fluctuations in matter during cosmic inflation. They are also considered possible candidates for dark matter, the unseen material that accounts for about 90% of matter in the Universe by mass.
As PBHs travel through space, some could pass through stars. Previous research has suggested that the intense tidal forces created by a PBH’s gravity during such an encounter might ignite a white dwarf, the compact remnant left by a low-mass star, and cause it to explode as a Type Ia supernova (SNe Ia).
Shing-Chi Leung, an assistant professor at SUNY Polytechnic Institute and visiting associate scientist at The University of Tokyo’s Kavli Institute for the Physics and Mathematics of the Universe (Kavli IPMU), led the research. The study also included Kavli IPMU Visiting Senior Scientist Ken’ichi Nomoto and Kavli IPMU Senior Fellow Alexander Kusenko.
The researchers examined the motion, light, and chemical signatures expected from supernovae produced through this proposed PBH-triggered pathway.
In an earlier study published in 2025, the group showed that explosions initiated by primordial black holes could produce SNe Ia that closely resemble those generated by standard Type Ia supernova models.
For the latest work, the researchers compared their models with the supernova remnants Tycho, Kepler, and 3C 397, as well as nearby explosions including SN 2011fe and SN 2012cg. They also examined chemical abundance patterns in stars throughout the Milky Way.
The results showed that PBH-triggered SNe Ia could reproduce several observed properties of these objects. By studying radioactive isotopes such as Ni-56 and Ni-57, together with stable elements including Mn and Ni, the researchers constrained the masses and metallicities (the amount of heavier elements present when a star formed, which provides clues to its age in cosmic history) of the stars that produced the explosions and remnants.
The researchers also modeled how this proposed explosion pathway could contribute to the chemical enrichment of the galaxy. Their results indicated that a non-zero fraction of Type Ia supernovae triggered by primordial black holes is needed to explain a chemical abundance trend observed among Milky Way stars.
“Our work suggests that some supernovae that we observe in the sky could be a result of PBHs. Therefore, even though we cannot directly observe these evasive entities, they leave many interesting clues in nature for us to probe their properties.” Leung said.
The researchers plan to broaden their investigation by examining how PBH-triggered explosions would affect the overall population of conventional supernovae and the combined rates of these short-lived astronomical events.
Reference: “Primordial Black Hole Triggered Type Ia Supernovae. II. Comparison with Supernova Remnants and Galactic Chemical Evolution” by Shing-Chi Leung, Seth Walther, Alexander Kusenko, Ken’ichi Nomoto and Tomoharu Suzuki, 15 June 2026,
The Astrophysical Journal

title: Scientists Test Natural Compounds Against Sarcoma: Which One Shows the Most Promise?
content:
A laboratory study identified curcumin as the plant compound offering the best balance of anticancer activity and safety against fibrosarcoma cells.
A plant compound can damage cancer cells in the laboratory yet still prove too toxic to become a useful treatment. That distinction emerged when researchers at Wroclaw Medical University and the University of Wroclaw compared curcumin, berberine, and several other natural substances known for their anti-inflammatory and anticancer properties.
The researchers tested five compounds: curcumin, berberine, biochanin A, cucurbitacin E, and CAPE (caffeic
phenethyl ester), which is found in propolis. They compared how each substance affected fibrosarcoma cells and healthy muscle cells.
Their investigation centered on the NF-κB signaling pathway, a system involved in inflammation, metabolism, cell survival, and cellular aging. “NF-κB acts like a central control switch that integrates cellular stress signals and determines whether a cell activates inflammatory pathways, fights for survival, or changes its metabolism,” explains Prof. Julita Kulbacka from the Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology at Wroclaw Medical University.
Cancer cells can exploit excessive NF-κB activity to survive and adjust to difficult conditions. However, healthy cells also depend on this pathway, meaning a potential treatment would need to regulate it carefully rather than shut it down entirely.
All five compounds interfered with mitochondrial function, limiting the cells’ ability to generate energy.
ATP, the main source of usable energy within cells, fell by approximately 83–92% in fibrosarcoma cells. In healthy muscle cells, the decline ranged from around 23–73%. The difference suggests that the cancer cells were more sensitive to disruptions in energy metabolism.
The treatments also altered mitophagy, the cellular process that removes damaged mitochondria.
“Berberine, cucurbitacin E and CAPE enhanced PINK1/PARKIN-dependent mitophagy in fibrosarcoma cells. Combined with the marked reduction in ATP levels, this indicates not a protective response but an overwhelmed adaptive mechanism leading to cellular senescence and death,” says Prof. Julita Kulbacka.
Each of the five compounds caused fibrosarcoma cells to develop features of cellular senescence. Senescent cells remain alive but permanently stop dividing.
Curcumin produced the strongest response. The share of senescent cancer cells rose from approximately 16.5% to more than 75%, while the other compounds increased the proportion to more than 66%.
Healthy muscle cells generally reacted less strongly, indicating that the compounds showed some selectivity toward cancer cells.
Cell viability tests found that curcumin and CAPE were the most selective against fibrosarcoma cells. Curcumin combined substantial anticancer activity and induction of senescence with a comparatively favorable safety profile.
“Our findings show that these natural compounds can selectively place a greater metabolic burden on cancer cells than on healthy cells by disrupting mitochondrial function and energy metabolism. Among the compounds tested, curcumin demonstrated the most balanced profile,” emphasizes Prof. Julita Kulbacka.
Berberine was also tolerated relatively well, although researchers said its effects on mitochondria in healthy muscle cells need further examination.
The researchers conducted an initial safety assessment using greater wax moth (Galleria mellonella) larvae as a toxicity model.
Curcumin and berberine were tolerated best. CAPE and cucurbitacin E produced higher mortality, while biochanin A was the most toxic of the compounds tested.
The results show why anticancer potency alone cannot determine whether a substance is a promising drug candidate. Researchers must also evaluate its effects on healthy tissues and the entire organism.
The findings do not show that curcumin, berberine, or any of the other compounds can currently treat sarcomas in people. The experiments used animal cell lines and a basic invertebrate toxicity model.
“Our findings come from laboratory experiments and preliminary tests in wax moth larvae. The next step is to evaluate these compounds in more advanced in vivo models and to better understand their mechanisms of action, optimal dosing and delivery methods,” notes Prof. Kulbacka.
The research nevertheless helps identify which compounds warrant additional study. It also underscores the need to judge natural anticancer agents by both their activity against cancer cells and their safety for healthy tissue and the organism as a whole.
Reference: “Modulation of NFκB Signaling by Natural Compounds in Sarcoma and Normal Muscle Models” by Justyna Radzka, Agnieszka Gizak, Dagmara Baczyńska, Adam Junka, Bartłomiej Dudek, Malwina Brożyna, Anna Szewczyk and Julita Kulbacka, 1 June 2026,
International Journal of Molecular Sciences
DOI: 10.3390/ijms27115025
The study was supported by the Statutory Subsidy Funds of the Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology no. SUBZ.D260.26.013.
